summary:
Quebec is a province of Canada and stands under Canada's national framework: federal criminal law and the federal human-rights regime apply in Quebec as in every other province. Provincially, the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has prohibited discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression since 2016, reaching employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Provincial enforcement machinery has produced a documented win for a trans visitor or resident. On 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

Quebec's rules on sex designation and identity documents were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial with 29 witnesses, the Quebec Superior Court (2021 QCCS 191) declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people; the Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision (2024 QCCA 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code.

Correctional placement in Quebec now turns on anatomy rather than gender identity. On 19 June 2025 Quebec's public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities; the directive was issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison. Advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This is a dated, province-specific reversal of the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

Statistics Canada's police-reported hate crime release of 30 March 2026 reports 4,882 hate crimes nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, with provincial rates ranging from 5.3 per 100,000 (Manitoba, Newfoundland and Labrador) to 16.0 (Ontario). No Quebec-specific rate figure appears in that release, so the record's assessment of Quebec at national parity rests on the absence of a divergent provincial figure rather than on a measured Quebec number. The underlying analysis of national police hate-crime data, including sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations, was published by Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

Consensual sexual activity between adults was decriminalised nationally in 1969, and effective 21 June 2019 (S.C. 2019, c. 25) Criminal Code section 159 was repealed, barring conviction for any historical sexual offence unless the act would constitute an offence if committed on the day the charge was laid; that repeal removed that consensual-sex criminal liability in Quebec.

Quebec created civil unions by amending the Civil Code in 2002, giving couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation the same effects as marriage in respect of family direction, parental authority, expenses, family residence, family patrimony and compensatory allowance, valid only within Quebec. Same-sex adoption was legalised in Quebec in 2002.

2021 census data cited by Éducaloi indicates that 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older, and 0.27% of those aged 15 to 34, identify as transgender.
tangentialFactors:
Quebec sits within a national picture in which police-reported hate crime rose 142% between 2018 and 2024 to a rate of 12.1 per 100,000, with eight provinces stable or declining in 2024; the release does not break out Quebec.

Other Canadian provinces have moved in the opposite direction on trans-related rules: Saskatchewan's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who request use of a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and Alberta in 2024 passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, then blocked court challenges with Bill 9 (Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025), also using the notwithstanding clause. A visitor moving between provinces should not assume Quebec's framework travels with them.

The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologised in December 2020 for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to address implicit bias and systemic barriers.

Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide in 2022, for minors and adults, and made subjecting anyone to it a crime under the Criminal Code.

Rankings of Canada's LGBT-friendliness are framed around gay-friendliness and sexuality rather than transgender people specifically: first (least dangerous) in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024.

A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 87.6% of respondents said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour. Separate sexuality-attitude figures, not transgender-specific, showed 2020 Pew Research support for social acceptance of homosexuality at 85% of the general population and 92% among ages 18-29, up from 80% in 2013.

Montreal's Gay Village is among the country's established gay areas, with Pride celebrated every summer in major cities with federal, provincial and municipal political participation.
localsOnly:
Transgender Quebecers can change their legal gender under provincial rules; the Civil Code provisions governing sex designation were declared invalid in 2021 and largely upheld on appeal in 2024, prompting legislative reform.

Discrimination complaints on gender identity or expression in areas of provincial responsibility run through the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms and the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal, which has awarded damages in a trans hiring case.

Transgender inmates in Quebec provincial custody are placed according to anatomical sex under the directive announced by the public security minister on 19 June 2025, reversing prior practice; advocates contend this breaches the Quebec Charter.

Quebec's 2002 civil union regime is valid only within Quebec and does not travel to other provinces.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 contains no Quebec-specific hate-crime rate, so the province's position relative to the 5.3 to 16.0 per 100,000 provincial range is unresolved in this record; the parity assessment rests on the absence of a divergent figure rather than a measured one.

Whether the 19 June 2025 correctional placement directive has been challenged in court, and with what outcome, is not sourced here; only the advocates' position that it violates the Quebec Charter is documented.

The specific Civil Code provisions invalidated in 2021 QCCS 191 and the terms of the resulting legislative reform are not set out in this inventory; the current wording of Quebec's sex-designation rules is unresolved.

The 0.14% and 0.27% transgender identification figures derive from 2021 census data as cited by Éducaloi and are not a current prevalence measure.
